title: Database Migrations (golang-migrate & goose)
summary: A database schema evolves over time, and every change must be **versioned, reproducible, and applied in the same order everywhere** — from a developer laptop to production. Migration tools like **golang-migrate** and **goose** solve this: you write ordered migration files (SQL or Go), the tool records which have run in a tracking table, and it applies only the missing ones. Master forward-only vs up/down, transactional vs non-transactional migrations, embedding migrations with `embed.FS`, and safe deploy ordering, and your schema changes stop being scary.

subtopics.title: Why versioned schema migrations exist
subtopics.explanation: A schema is code: it changes as features land, and those changes must apply identically on every machine and environment. Ad-hoc SQL run by hand drifts — one server gets a column another lacks. Migration tools give each change an ordered version and record applied versions in a table, so any database can be brought to a known state deterministically. This ordered, recorded history is the backbone every other migration topic here builds on.

subtopics.title: golang-migrate: up/down files & the version table
subtopics.explanation: golang-migrate uses paired files per version: `{version}_{name}.up.sql` and `.down.sql`. It stores the current version and a `dirty` flag in a `schema_migrations` table. `migrate up` applies pending up files in order; `migrate down` reverses using down files. You can drive it from the CLI or embed it as a library in your app. Understanding this file/version-table contract is what lets you reason about every up/down operation the tool performs.

subtopics.title: goose: SQL and Go migrations
subtopics.explanation: goose supports both `.sql` migrations (with `-- +goose Up` / `-- +goose Down` annotations) and Go migrations, where each migration is a registered Go function receiving a `*sql.Tx` — useful when a change needs application logic, not just SQL. Its tracking table is `goose_db_version`. You run it via the `goose` CLI or the library API. Go migrations are goose's differentiator, letting you express data transformations that pure SQL can't easily do.

subtopics.title: Embedding migrations with embed.FS
subtopics.explanation: Shipping loose `.sql` files beside a binary is fragile — the files can go missing in a container. Go's `embed.FS` compiles the migration directory into the binary, and both golang-migrate (via the `iofs` source) and goose (`goose.SetBaseFS`) can read from it. The app then migrates itself with no external files. Embedding is what turns 'migrations plus a binary' into a single self-contained artifact you can deploy anywhere.

subtopics.title: Transactional vs non-transactional migrations
subtopics.explanation: Most migrations run inside a transaction so a failure rolls back cleanly and never half-applies. But some statements can't run in a transaction — e.g. Postgres `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (which avoids locking a large table) must run outside one. goose has a `-- +goose NO TRANSACTION` directive and golang-migrate runs each file's statements as configured; you split such statements into their own migration. Knowing which changes must skip a transaction is what prevents both table-locking outages and 'cannot run inside a transaction block' errors.
subtopics.example:
-- goose: this migration must NOT be wrapped in a transaction.
-- +goose NO TRANSACTION
-- +goose Up
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email ON users (email);

-- +goose Down
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_users_email;

-- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids an exclusive lock on a big table,
-- but Postgres forbids it inside a transaction block.

subtopics.title: Safe production rollout ordering
subtopics.explanation: In a rolling deploy the old and new code run simultaneously, so schema changes must be backward compatible. The safe rule is 'migrate before rollout' for additive changes (add a nullable column, then deploy code that writes it) and 'expand/contract' for removals (deploy code that stops using a column, then drop it in a later migration). Never ship a migration that the currently-running old code can't tolerate. This ordering discipline is what makes migrations compatible with zero-downtime deploys instead of causing outages mid-rollout.

foundations.overview: Database migrations turn schema changes into ordered, versioned, replayable units. Tools like golang-migrate and goose keep a record of which versions a database has applied and run only the missing ones, so any environment can be brought to a known schema deterministically. The core insight is that migrations are code you commit alongside your app — reviewed, tested, and rolled out with the same discipline. Get versioning, transactionality, and rollout ordering right and schema evolution becomes routine instead of dangerous.
foundations.formalDefinition: A migration is a versioned, ordered transformation of a database schema (and sometimes its data). A migration tool maintains a version-tracking table (schema_migrations for golang-migrate, goose_db_version for goose), compares it to the set of migration files, and applies the pending forward migrations in version order — optionally reversing them via down migrations.
foundations.whyItMatters: Schema drift between environments and half-applied changes are among the most common causes of production incidents. Versioned migrations make schema changes reproducible, reviewable, and automatable in CI/CD, which is why nearly every serious backend service uses a migration tool.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of migrations like version control for your database. Each migration is a commit that moves the schema forward one step; the tool's version table is the HEAD pointer that says how far this particular database has advanced. Applying migrations is fast-forwarding to the latest commit; a down migration is a revert.
foundations.runtimePerspective: At startup or in a deploy step, the tool opens the database, reads the current version from its tracking table, sorts migration files by version, and executes each pending one — typically inside a transaction, updating the version (and clearing the dirty flag) as it goes. If a migration fails mid-way, the version is left marked dirty so the tool refuses to proceed until a human resolves it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Adding tables/columns/indexes, backfilling data, seeding reference data, and evolving schemas across microservices. Run as a CLI in a CI/CD deploy job, an init container/Job in Kubernetes, or embedded in the app binary and run at startup.
foundations.businessImpact: Reliable migrations enable safe, frequent releases; broken or unordered ones cause outages, data loss, and long incident post-mortems. Zero-downtime rollout ordering directly protects availability during deploys.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Migrations committed with code give reviewers visibility into schema changes, make environments reproducible, and let CI verify that up and down both work. They remove the class of bugs caused by 'someone ran SQL by hand'.
foundations.performanceImpact: Some migrations lock tables (adding a NOT NULL column with a default on old Postgres, or a plain CREATE INDEX), which can stall a busy service. Using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, batched backfills, and expand/contract patterns keeps migrations from causing latency spikes or downtime.
commonUseCases: Adding or altering tables, columns, and constraints in version order
Creating indexes safely (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, non-transactional)
Backfilling or transforming existing data (often a goose Go migration)
Running migrations in a CI/CD deploy step or Kubernetes init Job before rollout
Seeding reference/lookup data in a repeatable way

commonMisconceptions.myth: Down migrations make production rollbacks safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In production, down migrations are risky: they can destroy data (a DROP COLUMN loses the data) and the old code may still expect the new schema. Real recovery is usually a new forward migration or a restore, not a blind down.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can just run migrations any time relative to the deploy.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Order matters. In a rolling deploy old and new code coexist, so migrations must be backward compatible; you generally migrate additive changes BEFORE rollout and drop things only after all code stops using them (expand/contract).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every migration runs inside a transaction, so partial failure is impossible.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Some statements (e.g. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres) cannot run in a transaction. Those run without one and CAN partially fail, leaving the DB in an intermediate state that must be handled.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A 'dirty' migration just needs to be re-run.
commonMisconceptions.reality: golang-migrate refuses to run while dirty. You must fix the DB to a consistent state and use `force <version>` to set the correct version, then continue — blindly re-running can double-apply changes.

interactiveExamples.title: golang-migrate CLI: create, up, down, and inspect version
interactiveExamples.explanation: The CLI creates paired up/down files, applies them, and tracks state in schema_migrations. `migrate create` scaffolds a timestamped pair; `migrate up` applies pending files; `migrate version` shows the current version and dirty flag; `migrate down 1` reverses one step using the down file.

code.code:
# Scaffold a new versioned migration pair (creates .up.sql and .down.sql).
migrate create -ext sql -dir migrations -seq create_users
# => migrations/000001_create_users.up.sql
# => migrations/000001_create_users.down.sql

# Apply all pending migrations against a Postgres DB.
migrate -path migrations -database "postgres://app:pw@localhost:5432/app?sslmode=disable" up

# Show current version and whether the DB is dirty.
migrate -path migrations -database "$DB_URL" version

# Roll back exactly one migration (runs 000001_create_users.down.sql).
migrate -path migrations -database "$DB_URL" down 1
code.caption: The CLI records applied versions in schema_migrations; up applies pending files, down reverses them.
code.expectedOutput:
1
# (version prints 1; would print '1 (dirty)' if a migration failed mid-way)

interactiveExamples.title: Embed migrations in the binary and run them at startup
interactiveExamples.explanation: Using embed.FS plus golang-migrate's iofs source, the migration files are compiled into the binary. At startup the app runs m.Up(), ignoring ErrNoChange when already current. This makes the deployable a single self-contained artifact — no external SQL files to lose.

code.caption: embed.FS + iofs source compiles migrations into the binary so it migrates itself.

interactiveExamples.title: goose: a non-transactional CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY migration
interactiveExamples.explanation: Adding an index to a large, live table with a plain CREATE INDEX takes an exclusive lock and blocks writes. Postgres offers CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, but it cannot run inside a transaction. goose's `-- +goose NO TRANSACTION` directive tells goose to run this file outside a transaction so the statement is legal.

code.code:
-- 20260707120000_add_users_email_index.sql
-- +goose NO TRANSACTION
-- +goose Up
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_email ON users (email);

-- +goose Down
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_users_email;

# Apply it with the goose CLI (goose_db_version tracks state).
# goose -dir migrations postgres "$DB_URL" up
#
# Without NO TRANSACTION goose wraps the file in BEGIN/COMMIT and Postgres
# rejects it: ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block
code.caption: NO TRANSACTION lets CONCURRENTLY statements run; without it Postgres errors out.

checkpoints.prompt: In golang-migrate, what does the `dirty` flag in the schema_migrations table indicate?
options: A migration failed part-way and the tool won't proceed until it's resolved
There are pending migrations not yet applied
checkpoints.explanation: golang-migrate marks the version dirty when a migration fails mid-execution. While dirty, it refuses to run further migrations; you must bring the DB to a consistent state and use `force <version>` to clear it. Pending-but-not-applied is normal and is NOT the dirty state.

checkpoints.prompt: You call m.Up() but the database is already at the latest version. What does golang-migrate return, and how should idiomatic code treat it?
options: A generic error that should abort startup
migrate.ErrNoChange, which should be treated as success (already up to date)
nil always, even when nothing changed
A panic because there is nothing to apply
checkpoints.explanation: When there are no pending migrations, Up() returns migrate.ErrNoChange. Idiomatic code checks for it with errors.Is and treats it as a no-op success, so re-running migrations on an already-current DB is safe.

checkpoints.prompt: This goose SQL migration adds an index to a large live table but keeps causing a write outage during deploy. What's the root problem?
options: A plain CREATE INDEX takes an exclusive lock; it should use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY with -- +goose NO TRANSACTION
goose can't create indexes at all
The Down migration should recreate the index
checkpoints.explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX locks the table against writes for the whole build, causing an outage on a large table. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which builds without an exclusive lock — but it can't run in a transaction, so the file needs `-- +goose NO TRANSACTION`.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the golang-migrate library call so migrations already applied don't cause an error.
checkpoints.explanation: Up() returns migrate.ErrNoChange when the DB is already current. Guarding with `!errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrNoChange)` means you only propagate real failures and treat 'nothing to do' as success.

codeLab.title: Write a reusable golang-migrate runner that is safe to call repeatedly
codeLab.instructions: Implement `RunMigrations(sourceURL, dbURL string) error` using golang-migrate. It must build a migrate instance, call Up(), and treat migrate.ErrNoChange as success (return nil) while propagating all other errors. Calling it twice in a row on the same DB must not error.
hints: migrate.New(sourceURL, dbURL) returns a *migrate.Migrate; remember to defer m.Close().
Up() returns migrate.ErrNoChange when there is nothing to apply — that is not a real failure.
Use errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrNoChange) so the second call is a safe no-op.

codeLab.title: Serve embedded migrations to golang-migrate via iofs
codeLab.instructions: Given an embed.FS containing a `migrations` directory, implement `NewSource(fs embed.FS) (source.Driver, error)` that returns an iofs source driver rooted at 'migrations'. Then `MigrateEmbedded(fs embed.FS, dbURL string) error` must build a migrate instance from that source and run Up(), treating ErrNoChange as success.
hints: iofs.New(fs, "migrations") returns a source.Driver reading from the embedded FS.
Use migrate.NewWithSourceInstance("iofs", src, dbURL) — not migrate.New — because the source is an instance, not a URL.
As with any runner, guard Up() with !errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrNoChange).

debuggingLab.title: 'Dirty database version' blocks all further migrations
debuggingLab.symptom: A migration failed part-way in production (a bad SQL statement). Now every deploy fails at the migration step with: 'error: Dirty database version 5. Fix and force version.' No new migrations apply.

brokenCode.code:
# The deploy just keeps re-running `migrate up`, hoping it clears.
migrate -path migrations -database "$DB_URL" up
# => error: Dirty database version 5. Fix and force version.

# 000005_add_orders_status.up.sql (the one that failed):
#   ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL;  -- fails: existing rows have no value
#   CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status);   -- never ran

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: golang-migrate ran version 5, the ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL failed on existing rows (no default), and it marked schema_migrations dirty at version 5. While dirty, the tool refuses to apply anything. Blindly re-running `up` can't help and risks double-applying whatever DID succeed. You must inspect what actually applied, manually reconcile the DB to a known state, then `force` the version to the last cleanly-applied one before continuing.
commonMistakes: Re-running `migrate up` repeatedly, expecting the dirty flag to clear itself.
Blindly `force`ing to the failed version without checking what partially applied (risks double-apply).
Writing ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL with no DEFAULT on a table that already has rows.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Reconcile the DB by hand, force the version to the last good migration (4), fix the migration to be safe (nullable or with a default, then backfill), and re-run up.

solution.code:
# 1. Inspect what actually applied for version 5 (did the column get added?).
#    psql "$DB_URL" -c "\d orders"

# 2. Undo any partial change so the DB matches the end of version 4.
#    psql "$DB_URL" -c "ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS status;"

# 3. Clear the dirty flag by forcing to the last CLEAN version.
migrate -path migrations -database "$DB_URL" force 4

# 4. Fix migration 000005 to be safe on existing rows, e.g.:
#    ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending';

# 5. Re-run; it now applies version 5 cleanly.
migrate -path migrations -database "$DB_URL" up
solution.expectedOutput:
5/u add_orders_status (12.4ms)
# version is now 5 and no longer dirty

theory.question: Why do we use versioned schema migration tools instead of running SQL by hand, and how does the version-tracking table work?
theory.directAnswer: Hand-run SQL causes drift: environments end up with different schemas and there's no record of what ran. A migration tool gives each change an ordered version and records applied versions in a tracking table (schema_migrations for golang-migrate, goose_db_version for goose). On each run it compares that table to the migration files and applies only the pending ones in order, so any database can be deterministically brought to a known state. This makes schema changes reproducible, reviewable in code, and automatable in CI/CD.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An ordered, recorded history of schema changes plus a tool that applies the missing ones.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate schema drift and half-applied ad-hoc changes across environments.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The tool reads the current version from its tracking table, sorts files by version, and runs each pending forward migration, updating the version as it goes.

theory.whyImportant: Reproducible schema evolution is foundational to safe deploys and is a very common backend interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A CI deploy job runs `migrate up`; a fresh staging DB gets exactly the same schema as production because both replay the same versioned files.

followUps.question: What happens if two developers create migrations with the same version number?
followUps.answer: You get a conflict/ambiguous ordering; sequence numbers collide. Teams use timestamp-based versions (like goose) or coordinate sequence numbers, and CI should detect duplicates.

followUps.question: How does the tool know which migrations to skip?
followUps.answer: It reads the highest applied version (and per-version records) from its tracking table and only runs files with versions greater than the current one.

theory.question: Compare golang-migrate and goose. When would you reach for goose's Go migrations?
theory.directAnswer: Both are versioned SQL migration tools with a CLI and a library API. golang-migrate uses paired {version}_{name}.up.sql/.down.sql files, a schema_migrations table, and supports many databases and sources (file, iofs, S3, GitHub). goose uses single annotated SQL files (-- +goose Up/Down) OR Go migrations registered as functions, tracked in goose_db_version. You reach for goose's Go migrations when a change needs application logic that's awkward in pure SQL — e.g. reading rows, transforming them in Go (parsing, hashing, calling a library), and writing them back within the migration's transaction.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two popular Go migration tools with overlapping features and one key difference: goose supports Go migrations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different teams want different file conventions, and some data transformations can't be expressed cleanly in SQL.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: goose.AddMigration registers up/down Go funcs receiving *sql.Tx; goose runs the matching one inside a transaction when it reaches that version.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right tool and knowing when a data migration needs code, not SQL, is a practical engineering judgment interviewers probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Backfilling a `slug` column by slugifying titles with a Go library is trivial as a goose Go migration but painful as portable SQL.

followUps.question: Can golang-migrate do data transformations in Go?
followUps.answer: Not as a migration file — it runs SQL. You'd do complex transforms in application code or switch to goose Go migrations for in-migration logic.

followUps.question: What do both tools name their tracking tables?
followUps.answer: golang-migrate uses schema_migrations; goose uses goose_db_version.

theory.question: Why are down migrations risky in production, and what should you do instead when a deploy goes wrong?
theory.directAnswer: Down migrations are risky because they can be destructive and assume the environment is safe to reverse. A DROP COLUMN down migration permanently loses data; running a down while old code that depends on the new schema is still live can break that code. They're written for local development convenience, not production recovery. In production you usually roll FORWARD: write a new migration that corrects the problem, or if data is at risk, restore from backup/PITR. Combined with expand/contract sequencing, most changes never need a down at all.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The reverse operation of a migration, meant to undo a schema change.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So developers can iterate locally and step schemas back and forth during development.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The tool runs the .down.sql (or down Go func) for the current version and decrements the tracked version.

theory.whyImportant: Believing down migrations are a safe production rollback is a common cause of data loss; interviewers look for this nuance.
theory.realWorldExample: A team 'rolled back' by running down on a migration that dropped a column — the down recreated the column but the data was gone; they had to restore from backup.

followUps.question: So should you even write down migrations?
followUps.answer: Yes, for local dev and CI testing (apply up then down to verify reversibility), but don't rely on them as your production recovery plan.

followUps.question: What's the safe way to remove a column?
followUps.answer: Expand/contract: deploy code that stops using it, wait until no code references it, then drop it in a later migration once you're confident.

scenario.question: You must rename a heavily-used `users.name` column to `full_name` with zero downtime during a rolling deploy. How do you sequence the migrations and code changes?
scenario.directAnswer: Use expand/contract so old and new code can coexist. Step 1 (migration, before rollout): ADD COLUMN full_name, keeping name. Step 2 (deploy code): write to BOTH columns and read full_name-then-name as fallback. Step 3 (migration): backfill UPDATE users SET full_name = name WHERE full_name IS NULL, in batches to avoid long locks. Step 4 (deploy code): read/write only full_name. Step 5 (migration, after all instances are on new code): DROP COLUMN name. Each step is backward compatible with the previous running version, so no request ever hits a schema the running code can't handle.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A multi-step expand/contract sequence that avoids any moment where code and schema disagree.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Rolling deploys run old and new code simultaneously, so a single destructive rename would break one of them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Additive migration first, dual-write code, backfill, switch reads/writes, then contract by dropping the old column.

scenario.whyImportant: Zero-downtime schema changes are a core production skill; a naive single ALTER causes errors mid-rollout.
scenario.realWorldExample: Large services rename or split columns exactly this way, often behind a feature flag controlling the read/write path.

followUps.question: Why backfill in batches?
followUps.answer: A single huge UPDATE can lock rows and bloat the transaction/WAL; batching by primary key ranges keeps locks short and lets you throttle.

followUps.question: When is it finally safe to run the DROP COLUMN?
followUps.answer: Only after every running instance is on code that no longer references name, and you've verified via metrics/logs that nothing reads or writes it.

scenario.question: Your team embeds migrations and runs them at app startup. As you scale to many replicas, deploys sometimes fail with conflicting migration errors. What's happening and how do you fix the ordering?
scenario.directAnswer: Multiple replicas start at once and all try to run migrations concurrently, racing on the same database; you can get lock contention, dirty state, or duplicate-apply errors. The fix is to run migrations exactly once per deploy, separately from the app's normal startup: use a dedicated migration step — a Kubernetes init container/Job, a CI/CD deploy stage, or a leader-elected single runner — that completes BEFORE the new replicas start serving. golang-migrate takes a database lock to serialize runners, but the cleaner pattern is 'migrate first, then roll out': the deploy pipeline runs migrations as a gate, and only on success does it start/replace the app pods.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A concurrency and ordering problem where many instances try to migrate simultaneously.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Running migrations inside every replica's startup means N concurrent migrators against one DB.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Isolate migrations into a single pre-rollout step (Job/init container/CI stage) that must succeed before app pods serve traffic.

scenario.whyImportant: Getting migration ordering wrong in a multi-replica deploy causes flaky, hard-to-debug rollout failures.
scenario.realWorldExample: A Kubernetes deploy runs a migration Job; the Deployment's new pods only roll out after the Job succeeds, guaranteeing one ordered migration run.

followUps.question: Does golang-migrate protect against concurrent runners at all?
followUps.answer: It acquires an advisory database lock so concurrent runs serialize rather than corrupt state, but you still shouldn't rely on N racing migrators — run it once.

followUps.question: What ordering rule keeps this safe?
followUps.answer: Migrate before rollout for additive changes; only start new code once migrations that it depends on have completed successfully.

systemDesign.question: Design a database migration workflow for a Go microservice deployed to Kubernetes that must support zero-downtime deploys, be reproducible across environments, and handle failures safely.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Store migrations as versioned SQL files in the repo and embed them into the binary with embed.FS (so the artifact is self-contained). Run migrations as a dedicated, single, pre-rollout step — a Kubernetes Job (or init container gated by leader election) that runs `migrate up` and must succeed before the new app pods roll out ('migrate before rollout'). Design every migration to be backward compatible using expand/contract so old and new code coexist during the rolling update. Use transactions by default; split non-transactional statements (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) into their own NO TRANSACTION migration and batch large backfills. On failure, the deploy halts; a dirty version is resolved by an operator (inspect, reconcile, force to the last clean version) — recovery is roll-forward, not blind down. Seed reference data via idempotent seed migrations. In CI, test that up-then-down works and that migrations apply cleanly on a throwaway DB to catch drift early.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An end-to-end migration pipeline: versioned+embedded files, a single pre-rollout runner, backward-compatible changes, and a defined failure/recovery path.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Services need schema evolution that is reproducible, ordered, and safe during concurrent rolling deploys.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: CI validates migrations; the deploy runs them once as a gate; app pods roll out only on success; expand/contract keeps each step compatible.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It combines every operational concern — reproducibility, ordering, concurrency, failure handling — that real backend systems and interviews care about.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A Helm-based deploy runs a pre-upgrade migration Job; the Deployment updates only after the Job completes, and migrations are embedded so rollback of the binary doesn't lose the SQL.

followUps.question: Where should the migration runner live — app startup or a separate step?
followUps.answer: A separate step (Job/init container/CI stage) so exactly one ordered run happens per deploy, not N racing runs from every replica.

followUps.question: How do you keep migrations reproducible across dev/staging/prod?
followUps.answer: Commit the files, embed them in the binary, and run the same versioned set everywhere; CI applies them to a throwaway DB to detect drift.

followUps.question: How do you handle a migration that must not lock a huge table?
followUps.answer: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a NO TRANSACTION migration and backfill data in bounded batches to keep locks short.

coding.question: Implement a function that runs embedded golang-migrate migrations and is safe to call on an already-current database. Signature: `func Migrate(fs embed.FS, dbURL string) error`.
coding.thoughtProcess: The migrations live in an embed.FS, so I need the iofs source rather than a file:// URL. Build the source with iofs.New(fs, "migrations"), then migrate.NewWithSourceInstance to attach a database driver (imported for side effects). Call Up(), and because re-running on a current DB returns migrate.ErrNoChange, I must treat that as success with errors.Is. Close the instance to release the DB lock.
coding.lineByLine: iofs.New(fs, "migrations") builds a source.Driver that reads the embedded migrations directory. NewWithSourceInstance wires that source to the postgres database driver (imported blank for its init side effect) using dbURL. defer m.Close() releases the advisory lock and file handles. Up() applies pending migrations; ErrNoChange (nothing pending) is filtered with errors.Is so a second call is a clean no-op, and any other error is returned.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the number of pending migration statements executed.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the embedded files already compiled into the binary.

followUps.question: Why NewWithSourceInstance instead of migrate.New?
followUps.answer: migrate.New takes URL strings; an embed.FS is an in-memory source instance, so you must pass it via NewWithSourceInstance.

followUps.question: Why does defer m.Close() matter here?
followUps.answer: golang-migrate holds a database advisory lock while open; not closing it can block the next migration runner.

coding.question: Write a goose Go migration that backfills a `slug` column from `title` using Go string logic, with a matching down. Register it with goose.AddMigration.
coding.thoughtProcess: A goose Go migration is a pair of funcs taking *sql.Tx, registered in init via goose.AddMigration. The up should query rows, compute a slug in Go (lowercase, spaces to hyphens), and UPDATE each row — all on the tx so it commits atomically. The down should null the column out to reverse. I iterate rows, close the rows before issuing updates (or collect first) to avoid using a connection mid-iteration.
coding.lineByLine: init registers the up/down pair with goose so it runs at the migration's version. slugify does the Go-side transform SQL can't do cleanly. upBackfillSlugs queries rows needing a slug, scans them into a slice, and crucially closes rows before running updates (you can't run new statements on the same tx while a result set is open). It then updates each row on the tx so everything commits atomically. downBackfillSlugs reverses by nulling the column.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the rows needing a slug.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the buffered records (batch it for very large tables).

followUps.question: Why buffer rows into a slice before updating?
followUps.answer: database/sql can't run a new query/exec on a connection while a Rows result set is still open on it; buffer first (or use a separate connection/batch).

followUps.question: How would you handle millions of rows?
followUps.answer: Process in bounded batches by id range across multiple migrations or a background job, to keep transactions and locks short.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep migrations as versioned files in the repo and embed them with embed.FS so the deployable is self-contained. Run them as a dedicated pre-rollout step (Kubernetes Job, init container, or CI/CD stage), never as N racing app replicas. Design every change to be backward compatible via expand/contract, and separate schema migrations from data backfills so each stays reviewable and reversible in dev.
productionDeepDive.performance: Beware locking migrations: plain CREATE INDEX and some ALTER TABLE variants take exclusive locks that stall a busy service. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (non-transactional), add columns without a rewrite where possible, and backfill in bounded batches to keep transactions and WAL growth small. Long single-statement backfills can pin autovacuum and bloat the table.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Migrations must run exactly once per deploy. golang-migrate takes a database advisory lock so concurrent runners serialize instead of corrupting state, but the correct pattern is a single runner (Job/leader election). Non-transactional migrations can partially apply, so make them idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS) so a retry is safe.
productionDeepDive.reliability: A failed migration leaves golang-migrate dirty and refuses to proceed; recovery is inspect -> reconcile the DB -> force the last clean version -> re-run, never blind re-run. Prefer roll-forward fixes over destructive down migrations in prod, and keep backups/PITR for changes that touch data. Test up-and-down in CI on a throwaway database to catch broken migrations before deploy.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log the version before and after each run and whether the DB was dirty; emit a metric/event for migration duration and outcome so slow or failing migrations are visible. Alert on dirty state and on migrations exceeding a duration budget (a sign of a locking/backfill problem). Record who/what deploy triggered the run for audit.
productionDeepDive.security: Run migrations with a database role that has DDL privileges, distinct from the app's least-privilege runtime role, and rotate/scope those credentials. Never log full connection strings or embed secrets in migration files. Review migrations like code — a stray DROP or a missing WHERE in a backfill can be catastrophic — and require approvals for destructive changes.

caseStudies.problem: Adding an index to a large orders table with a plain CREATE INDEX locked writes and caused an outage during deploy.
caseStudies.solution: Moved to CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a dedicated NO TRANSACTION migration and gated it behind a pre-rollout Job.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: CONCURRENTLY is slower and can leave an invalid index on failure that must be dropped and retried, but it avoids the exclusive lock.
caseStudies.lessons: Index and lock-heavy migrations need non-transactional, concurrent strategies; test them against production-sized data.

caseStudies.company: Multi-replica service embedding migrations at startup
caseStudies.problem: Every replica ran migrations on boot, racing the DB and occasionally leaving a dirty version during deploys.
caseStudies.solution: Extracted migrations into a single Kubernetes Job that must succeed before the Deployment's new pods roll out ('migrate before rollout').
caseStudies.tradeoffs: One extra deploy step and a strict ordering dependency, but a single deterministic migration run.
caseStudies.lessons: Migrate once per deploy as a gate; don't rely on many concurrent app instances to migrate correctly.

keyTakeaways: Migrations are versioned, ordered schema changes; the tool records applied versions in a tracking table (schema_migrations / goose_db_version) and applies only the pending ones so every environment converges to a known state.
golang-migrate uses paired up/down .sql files and a CLI+library API; goose adds annotated SQL and Go migrations (functions on *sql.Tx) for changes that need application logic like data backfills.
Embed migrations with embed.FS (iofs source for golang-migrate, SetBaseFS for goose) so the binary is a self-contained, deployable artifact with no loose SQL files.
Most migrations run in a transaction, but statements like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY must run non-transactionally in their own migration to avoid locking large tables.
Run migrations once per deploy as a pre-rollout gate and make changes backward compatible via expand/contract, so old and new code coexist safely during a rolling deploy.
A failed migration leaves the DB dirty; resolve by reconciling and forcing the last clean version, and prefer roll-forward over destructive down migrations in production.
